correctness.rationale: For every fixed C^4 strictly positively curved constant-width oval, constant width forces a complete 1D manifold of unique opposite-normal diameter pairs. The Euclidean distance has a uniform negative transverse quadratic coefficient ρ(θ)ρ(θ+π)/(2w), and the exact independent arclength-angle Jacobian is ρ(θ1)ρ(θ2)/(πw)^2. Integrating its root intervals yields the stated 2√2/π normalized Hellinger coefficient with O_K(ε/w) remainder. Cauchy–Schwarz proves exact circle rigidity; the positive 3-fold curvature-radius construction solves a periodic support equation and realizes every positive affinity, with 0 an unattained infimum. The supplied checker independently tests the finite-ε probability and local quadratic coefficient; it is not substituted for the all-oval proof.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: A random line through a convex body or a fixed circle with an anisotropic endpoint law is not equivalent to two arclength-uniform points on a noncircular constant-width boundary. The latter has a continuously parametrized diametral manifold but a nonconstant transverse distance Hessian, which introduces the reciprocal square root of antipodal curvature products. The corresponding Hellinger functional cannot be obtained by substituting a sampling density into the fixed-circle formula.

originality.rationale: The exact coefficient couples independently sampled arclength endpoint densities to a variable metric transverse-Hessian factor, giving the antipodal Hellinger affinity. The full 2006 circle result has a fixed circular distance Hessian and cannot imply the variable-curvature normalization; constant-width curvature papers do not compute probabilities. Two highly relevant published mathematical findings were inspected in full: the ellipse result has only a finite set of diametral configurations at fixed eccentricity, and the tangent-polygon result concerns large random circumscribed areas rather than independently sampled chord endpoints. The normalized coefficient rigidity, exact Hellinger deficit, and full sharp range are not statements or corollaries of those compared results. This is a bounded literature assessment, not exhaustive priority certification.

value.rationale: Constant-width curves share exactly the same width and perimeter, so a natural Euclidean boundary-pair measurement that distinguishes their antipodal curvature structure is mathematically motivated. The theorem identifies the sharp coefficient not merely as a formal integral but as the Hellinger affinity of opposite-normal curvature measures, yields quantitative TV stability and a circle-only equality case, and determines the entire nontrivial coefficient range with explicit smooth realizations. It detects an intrinsic geometric mismatch invisible to width/perimeter and is distinct from a fixed-shape exercise or small numerical improvement.
